'''Markov renewal processes''' are a class of [[stochastic process|random processes]] in probability and statistics that generalize the class of [[Markov property|Markov]] [[jump process|jump processes]]. Other classes of random processes, such as [[Markov chain|Markov chains]] and [[Poisson process|Poisson processes]], can be derived as special cases among the class of Markov renewal processes, while Markov renewal processes are special cases among the more general class of [[Renewal theory|renewal processes]].

==Definition==
[[File:Marked point process.png|thumb|365x365px|An illustration of a Markov renewal process]]
In the context of a jump process that takes states in a state space <math>\mathrm{S}</math>, consider the set of random variables <math>(X_n,T_n)</math>, where <math>T_n</math> represents the jump times and <math>X_n</math> represents the associated states in the sequence of states (see Figure). Let the sequence of inter-arrival times <math>\tau_n=T_n-T_{n-1}</math>. In order for the sequence <math>(X_n,T_n)</math> to be considered a Markov renewal process the following condition should hold:

<math>
\begin{align}
& \Pr(\tau_{n+1}\le t, X_{n+1}=j\mid(X_0, T_0), (X_1, T_1),\ldots, (X_n=i, T_n)) \\[5pt]
= {} & \Pr(\tau_{n+1}\le t, X_{n+1}=j\mid X_n=i)\, \forall n \ge1,t\ge0, i,j \in \mathrm{S}
\end{align}
</math>

==Relation to other stochastic processes==
# Let <math>X_n</math> and <math>T_n</math> be as defined in the previous statement. Defining a new stochastic process <math>Y_t:=X_n</math> for <math>t \in [T_n,T_{n+1})</math>, then the process <math>Y_t</math> is called a '''semi-Markov process''' as it happens in a [[continuous-time Markov chain]]. The process is Markovian only at the specified jump instants, justifying the name '''''semi'''''-Markov.<ref>{{cite book|last=Medhi|first=J.|title=Stochastic processes|year=1982|publisher=Wiley & Sons|location=New York|isbn=978-0-470-27000-4}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Ross|first=Sheldon M.|title=Stochastic processes.|year=1999|publisher=Routledge.|location=New York [u.a.]|isbn=978-0-471-12062-9|edition=2nd}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Barbu|first=Vlad Stefan|title=Semi-Markov chains and hidden semi-Markov models toward applications: their use in reliability and DNA analysis|year=2008|publisher=Springer|location=New York|isbn=978-0-387-73171-1|author2=Limnios, Nikolaos}}</ref> (See also: [[hidden semi-Markov model]].)
# A semi-Markov process (defined in the above bullet point) in which all the holding times are [[exponential distribution|exponentially distributed]] is called a [[continuous-time Markov chain]]. In other words, if the inter-arrival times are exponentially distributed and if the waiting time in a state and the next state reached are independent, we have a continuous-time Markov chain.
#:<math> \begin{align}
& \Pr(\tau_{n+1}\le t, X_{n+1}=j\mid(X_0, T_0), (X_1, T_1),\ldots, (X_n=i, T_n)) \\[3pt]
= {} & \Pr(\tau_{n+1}\le t, X_{n+1}=j\mid X_n=i) \\[3pt]
= {} & \Pr(X_{n+1}=j\mid X_n=i)(1-e^{-\lambda_i t}), \text{ for all } n \ge1,t\ge0, i,j \in \mathrm{S}, i \ne j
\end{align}
</math>
# The sequence <math>X_n</math> in the Markov renewal process is a '''discrete-time [[Markov chain]]'''. In other words, if the time variables are ignored in the Markov renewal process equation, we end up with a [[discrete-time Markov chain]].
#:<math>\Pr(X_{n+1}=j\mid X_0, X_1, \ldots, X_n=i)=\Pr(X_{n+1}=j\mid X_n=i)\, \forall n \ge1, i,j \in \mathrm{S} </math>
# If the sequence of <math>\tau</math>s is independent and identically distributed, and if their distribution does not depend on the state <math>X_n</math>, then the process is a '''renewal'''. So, if the states are ignored and we have a chain of iid times, then we have a renewal process.
#:<math>\Pr(\tau_{n+1}\le t\mid T_0, T_1, \ldots, T_n)=\Pr(\tau_{n+1}\le t)\, \forall n \ge1, \forall t\ge0 </math>
